ModelCharacter: A distinctly American answer to the 1970s Taiwan trawler: the Californian 34 LRC combines traditional trawler styling and excellent low-speed economy with a solid-fiberglass modified-V hull capable of true planing speeds when fitted with larger diesels. Wide side decks, a lower helm and surprising two-stateroom availability make it unusually versatile for 34 feet.
DesignLineage: Jule Marshall and Myrna Elliott developed Californian Yachts around the idea of building faster, moderately priced American trawler-style cruisers rather than copying slow Asian imports.
The 34 LRC followed the successful 42 LRC and became one of Californian's best-known models, with more than 200 built during the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Unlike most traditional trawlers, the 34 uses a modified-V hull with nearly flat aft sections, allowing either 7-knot economical operation with small diesels or roughly 16–20-knot cruising with larger engine packages.
The larger 38 LRC Sedan continues the same trawler-profile/modified-V design philosophy rather than representing a fundamentally different brand branch.
OwnershipCharacter: A relatively straightforward twin-shaft cruiser with strong fiberglass construction and very little exterior teak. Engine packages vary dramatically, so a low-powered Perkins boat and a Caterpillar-powered fast cruiser have very different fuel, performance and maintenance profiles; decks, windows, tanks and decades of owner modifications remain major survey items.

Strengths: Lower air draft and windage than the Troll
Single-diesel shaft simplicity with protected running gear
Excellent lower-helm visibility and compact couple-cruising footprint
Same efficient Keelform hull and owner-community support as the Troll
Weaknesses: Small cockpit, narrow side decks, compact wet head, limited storage and privacy, and no flybridge helm.
CommonProblems: Inspect deck and window bedding, cored structure around penetrations, fuel and water tanks, exhaust and raw-water systems, steering and shaft gear, and the condition of original or replacement diesel installations.
TypicalMission: Couple-focused inland-waterway, Great Loop and protected coastal cruising where low profile and lower-helm operation matter more than flybridge space.
AvoidIf: You specifically want a flybridge or upper outdoor helm
You need multiple private cabins or large-family accommodation
You require large cockpit or liveaboard storage volume
Overview: The Camano 28/31 Gnome is the no-flybridge sistership to the Camano Troll, using the same Bob Warman Keelform hull, 28-foot hull length and roughly 31-foot overall envelope. Its lower profile removes the upper helm and associated ladder, windage and flybridge maintenance while retaining the single-diesel shaft drive, bright deckhouse and couple-oriented interior. The Gnome was discontinued early in the family’s production, making it substantially rarer than the Troll.

SoloHandling.Summary: Compact dimensions, strong visibility and single-shaft propulsion support owner operation; docking conditions and thruster fit still matter.

ModelCharacter: A large raised-aft-deck Grand Banks designed around interior and entertaining volume rather than the working cockpit of the 49 Classic. DesignLineage: Derived from the Grand Banks 49 Classic family but differentiated by its raised aft-deck platform.

The 49 MY occupied the upper end of the Heritage-style range before later larger Motor Yacht and Aleutian models expanded the brand.
OwnershipCharacter: Best treated as a substantial liveaboard/cruising yacht. Twin engines, three heads, very large tankage and multiple accommodation zones demand professional-scale maintenance planning even though the underlying systems remain conventional by motor-yacht standards.

ModelCharacter: A compact Downeast-style diesel express built around a large cockpit, low air draft and useful cruising speed rather than trawler-style interior volume. It is a weekend cruiser that can fish, dive or travel efficiently without the height and windage of a flybridge boat.
DesignLineage: Introduced in 1998 as Mainship moved its single-diesel efficiency formula into a Downeast-style express cruiser.
A hardtop Pilot Sedan sister model followed in 1999 on the same basic platform.
The 2003 Series II update revised the cabin, shortened the keel, added a propeller tunnel and typically used higher-output Yanmar power.
The larger Mainship 34 Pilot was an enlarged derivative rather than the same hull.
OwnershipCharacter: Relatively straightforward for a diesel cruiser: one engine, direct shaft drive, good cockpit engine access and modest hotel systems. The main trade is limited cabin/storage volume for extended living, while Series I versus Series II hull details matter when comparing examples.

Established hull lineage that continued into the 39 and 40
Weaknesses: Engine room layout requires crawling to service outboard components.
CommonProblems: Molded step gelcoat cracking, high-amp alternator belt wear.
TypicalMission: Extended regional cruising, loops, and serious multi-week island hopping.

You require twin-engine redundancy
You want compact-boat operating and haul-out costs
Overview: The Nordic Tug 37 introduced the builder’s midsize two-stateroom pilothouse platform in 1998. The same basic hull later evolved into the Nordic Tug 39 and then the Nordic Tug 40.

ModelCharacter: A substantial midsize Nordic Tug that preserves the brand's single-engine efficiency and commercial-looking pilothouse while providing true extended-cruising room. It is large enough for two couples yet remains comparatively simple mechanically.
DesignLineage: Introduced in the late 1990s as Nordic Tugs expanded beyond the 26/32 family.
The 37 uses a solid-fiberglass semi-displacement hull with a full prop-protecting keel.
Later 37s integrated the formerly bolt-on swim step into the hull, lengthening the effective waterline.
The same family was renamed/evolved into the Nordic Tug 39 for the 2013–2015 generation.
OwnershipCharacter: A strong fit for serious cruising couples who want space and weather protection without twin engines. Systems and displacement are substantial enough that annual maintenance and marina costs are materially higher than on the 32/34.

DesignLineage: The Nimbus 365 Coupé was introduced for the 2011/2012 model period and won European Powerboat of the Year 2012.
It established the modern Nimbus 'sidewalk' Coupé architecture later used by the 305 and 405 Coupé.
The model has undergone styling, glazing and systems refinements while retaining the same core identity.
Single Volvo D6 and twin D4 shaft-drive configurations have both been factory-offered.

Single-shaft versions are simpler; twin-shaft versions add redundancy and cost. Heating, sunroofs, glazing and substantial domestic systems make it a real long-stay cruiser rather than a minimalist boat.

ModelCharacter: A modern 10-foot-beam diesel sedan cruiser with an unusually open, light-filled cabin, convertible cockpit seating and enough volume for extended couple cruising while remaining transportable with permits.
DesignLineage: The R-29 S succeeded the earlier R-29 Classic with a new, more contemporary cabin and interior architecture.
S means Sedan—the hardtop/lower-helm version of the current R-29 family.
The R-29 CB shares the same core hull and accommodations but adds a full upper command bridge.
Both current versions use single Volvo D4 diesel inboard propulsion.

ModelCharacter: A pivotal Sabre model launched in 2012 around pod propulsion, resin-infused construction and a fully enclosed salon that opens dramatically to the cockpit. It preserved Downeast exterior character while moving Sabre decisively toward quiet joystick-controlled, all-weather luxury cruising.
DesignLineage: The first Sabre 38 Salon Express launched in July 2012.
It was designed from the outset around close-coupled pod drives rather than adapting a conventional shaft hull.
The 38 SE followed the same pod-drive design movement as the Sabre 48 Salon Express introduced in 2011.
In 2026 Sabre reintroduced the 38 Salon Express with Volvo Penta DPI sterndrive propulsion, creating a significant new drivetrain generation within the same model identity.
OwnershipCharacter: Exceptionally refined and easy to maneuver, but pod-drive generations carry higher specialist service costs than straight shafts. The 2026 DPI version changes that ownership equation materially, so propulsion generation should be explicit when comparing listings.
